clue.text: Difficult time with some nasty shocks?

definitions.text: Difficult time with some nasty shocks?

parts.words: Difficult time with some nasty shocks?
parts.note: the nasty shocks read like jolts of bad news, but a shock is also a thick mass of hair, so the clue pictures a frustrating day spent with unruly locks

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a rough patch full of unpleasant surprises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shocks' wants to mean upsets; it means heads of hair, and the phrase names a day when everything goes wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a day of general frustration, literally one when your hairstyle refuses to behave.

clue.text: Foreign capital needs a new leader too

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Foreign capital needs a new leader too' (4) for ALSO: OSLO with its leading O replaced by A gives ASLO, not ALSO, and no other capital or reading found builds ALSO; clue may be garbled as held.
annotationWithheld.clue: Foreign capital needs a new leader too

clue.text: Punch given by rugby player without hesitation

indicators.note: without here means minus, so the hesitation sound is dropped from the player's position

parts.note: a hooker is the front-row forward who ... the ball back in a scrum
er is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A rugby player throws a blow without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' tells you to take ER out of HOOKER. In rugby the hooker is the player in the middle of the front row of the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A hook is a boxing blow thrown with a bent arm from the side.

clue.text: International man may receive many letters

definitions.note: the definition describes what the office tray does, standing in for the tray itself

parts.note: Ray is a man's first name

explanation.surface: A man on the international stage gets plenty of fan mail.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the thing that may receive many letters is the desk tray for incoming post.
explanation.definitionFit: An office tray for incoming post is where letters pile up awaiting attention.

clue.text: According to book, better speed possibly leads to anger

definitions.note: the definition is the general category, a reference book

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of better speed might be arranged in some other order

parts.note: rage is fierce anger

explanation.surface: A rule book apparently says that driving faster makes people cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges the eleven letters of 'better speed', and 'leads to' puts the anger word after them. 'According to' only links: doing something 'according to Debrett's' means doing it properly. Debrett's is the British guide to the aristocracy and etiquette.
explanation.definitionFit: Debrett's is a long-running British reference work listing titled families, the standard guide to rank and manners.

clue.text: Plant that's unknown, something pointed

parts.note: y is one of the letters used for an unknown quantity in algebra
an arrow has a sharp tip and points the way

explanation.surface: A botanist describes a mysterious specimen with a sharp tip.
explanation.walkthrough: Algebra's unknowns x, y and z give the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarrow is a flowering herb with feathery leaves and flat white flower heads.

clue.text: What's milky? It's quite different, this nightcap

indicators.note: quite different says the letters of the opening words are to come out in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone offered a milky bedtime drink protests that what they have in mind is something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite different' rearranges the letters of WHATS MILKY; the 's counts here as an S. 'It's' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A single-grain Scotch is a classic bedtime drink, the opposite of warm milk.

clue.text: Second-rate Greek character?

definitions.meaning: a grade marking work as second class, below alpha
the second letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.definitionFit: A beta mark is a second-class grade, and the same name belongs to the Greek letter after alpha.

clue.text: Desk one found in various rectories

indicators.note: found in says the letter for one sits inside the other letters
various suggests the letters of rectories in assorted arrangements

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A writing desk turns up in several vicarages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various' rearranges RECTORIES and 'found in' puts I inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: An escritoire is a writing desk with drawers and a fold-down flap.

clue.text: Gun provided by a man whose suaveness is tedious?

definitions.meaning: a firearm whose barrel has no rifling inside

definitions.text: a man whose suaveness is tedious?
definitions.meaning: a polished, smooth-talking man who nonetheless bores everyone

explanation.definitionFit: A smoothbore is a firearm with an unrifled barrel; split in two the words describe a sleek but dull person.

clue.text: About to be put into the street, unwelcome person may hear this

indicators.note: to be put into tells us the short word for about goes inside the street abbreviation

parts.note: St is the usual abbreviation for street
ca, short for circa, means about with dates

explanation.surface: An unwanted guest is about to be thrown out onto the street.
explanation.walkthrough: CA (circa) goes into ST. The definition is the word shouted to send someone away.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a curt order to go away, the sort of thing shouted at an intruder.

clue.text: Politician in Ireland with a policy to set the fashion

indicators.note: in places the member of parliament inside the name for Ireland

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland
MP stands for Member of Parliament
a party line is its official policy

explanation.surface: An Irish politician with a clear policy sets the trend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does the inserting and 'with' joins the policy word on. 'Set the fashion' looks like a verb phrase, but 'fashion' is a noun here: the empire line is a dress style.
explanation.definitionFit: The empire line is a dress style with a high waist just under the bust, popular in Napoleon's era.

clue.text: Arrived to meet destiny in romantic place

parts.note: came is the past tense of come, so it means arrived
one's lot is one's fate or destiny

explanation.surface: Someone arrives somewhere romantic to meet their fate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to meet' just links the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur's court in the medieval romances is the legendary seat of chivalry.

clue.text: Outside church provides refreshment for fisherman maybe

indicators.note: outside says the catering word goes round the church abbreviation

parts.note: to cater is to provide food and drink

explanation.surface: A churchyard stall serves drinks to a passing angler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' looks like it describes the church; it tells you to wrap the catering word round it. 'maybe' shows the fisherman is only one example of someone who catches.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who catches something, such as fish, is a catcher; an angler is one example.

clue.text: Malign a duke participating in ceasefire

indicators.note: participating in places the article and the abbreviation for duke inside the ceasefire word

parts.note: a truce is an agreed halt in fighting

explanation.surface: A nobleman is slandered while taking part in peace talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'participating in' puts A and D inside TRUCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To traduce someone is to speak badly of them and damage their reputation.

clue.text: Explosive device always being found in old city

parts.note: a bomb is an explosive device
ay, also spelt aye, is an old word for always

explanation.surface: A bomb is always turning up in an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being found in' just links. AY is an old poetic word for 'always'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumbai was formerly known by this name, so it is the old name of the Indian city.

clue.text: Spiteful message that may well put off intruders

definitions.meaning: a telegram, or wire, with barbs in it, meaning a cutting communication

definitions.text: that may well put off intruders
definitions.meaning: spiky fencing strung along walls and fences to deter trespassers

explanation.definitionFit: A wire is a telegram and barbed means cutting, so a hurtful note; the same words name spiky fencing that deters trespassers.

clue.text: Artist comes in accompanied by some looking pale and thin

definitions.note: plural-looking phrase standing for one ghostly figure, as if 'someone looking pale and thin'

indicators.note: comes in says the letters for the artist enter the other word

parts.note: with means accompanied by
RA, Royal Academician, is a standard abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: An artist arrives with a group who all look gaunt and wan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes in' does the inserting, and RA (Royal Academician) is the usual crossword artist. Read the definition as 'someone looking pale and thin'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wraith is a ghost, or a very thin, pale person who looks like one.

clue.text: Pour in a beastly fashion

parts.note: pour means rain heavily, and the beastly fashion points to two kinds of pet animal falling from the sky in the idiom

explanation.surface: Something is poured out in a nasty way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beastly' seems to mean nasty, but it means 'involving animals'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to rain very heavily, as if animals were falling from the sky.

clue.text: No longer always having time to enter the city

parts.note: ex means former, no longer

indicators.note: to enter puts the letter for time inside the poetic word for always

parts.note: e'er, a contraction of ever, means always

explanation.surface: Someone who no longer lives there always takes time to get into town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to enter' puts T inside E'ER. The city is Exeter, the county town of Devon in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeter is a cathedral city in Devon, England.

clue.text: Feel remorse, being shut up for the second time?

parts.note: re- as a prefix means again, so for a second time
pent means penned or shut up, as in pent-up

explanation.surface: Someone locked up twice comes to regret their crimes.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as RE-PENT, 'penned in again'.
explanation.definitionFit: To repent is to feel sorry for one's sins and resolve to change.

clue.text: Society — in short what is it? Contemptible!

parts.note: S is an abbreviation for society; 'in short' signals the shortening
asks what the letter S looks like: it is a shape full of bends

explanation.surface: A cynic dismisses society with a scornful rhetorical question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' turns 'Society' into S, and 'what is it?' asks what that letter is like: curvy, the shape of an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Scurvy as an adjective is an old word for mean or despicable, as in a scurvy knave.

clue.text: Is climbing blunder on a Spanish range?

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means read upwards, so the word is goes in backwards

parts.note: to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A mountaineer wonders whether a climb in Spain was a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns IS into SI, as this answer reads downwards. 'on' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Sierra is the Spanish word for a jagged mountain chain, as in the Sierra Nevada.

clue.text: Right always? That is just a dream!

parts.note: ever means always, as in ever hopeful
ie stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs that being permanently right is only a fantasy.
explanation.walkthrough: IE is the abbreviation for Latin id est, 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a daydream, a state of being lost in pleasant thoughts.

clue.text: Wife's success creating a church feast

parts.note: a hit is a success

explanation.surface: A wife's triumph leads to a parish celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 's just links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitsun, the Christian festival of Pentecost, is often shortened to its first syllable.

clue.text: Firm requirement before surgery

definitions.meaning: going without food beforehand, as patients must before an operation

explanation.definitionFit: Fast means fixed, as in stuck fast, and also a period without food, which patients are told to keep before an operation.

clue.text: Old soldier embraced by weaker novices

indicators.note: embraced by says the soldier sits inside the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A veteran is welcomed by the less able recruits.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is 'embraced by' weaKER Novices.
explanation.definitionFit: A kern was a lightly armed Irish or Scottish foot soldier of the Middle Ages.

clue.text: Second match — rarer game, I fancy

indicators.note: fancy here suggests imagining the letters of rarer game and I in another order

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a return game is an uncommon fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges RARER GAME plus I. 'match' looks sporting but means marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A second marriage is a new match after the first has ended.

clue.text: Carol in the grass

definitions.meaning: Sir Carol, the British film director of The Third Man
a tall waterside plant of the grass family

explanation.definitionFit: Sir Carol Reed directed The Third Man, and the same surname is a tall marsh plant of the grass family.

clue.text: Second person died holding a gun in Kray's territory

indicators.note: holding says the archaic pronoun and the death abbreviation wrap round the weapon

parts.note: thee is the old second-person pronoun
a Sten is a British submachine gun

explanation.surface: A gangland killing with a gun on the Krays' patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' does the wrapping. 'Second person' means grammar, not a second human being. The Kray twins ran organised crime in London's East End in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kray twins were gangsters who controlled this working-class district of east London in the 1960s.
